opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more interesting shifts in how people build robot systems.

If you go back a few years, the standard robotics stack was very modular: a perception module, then state estimation, then a planner, then a motion planner, then a low-level controller, often with hand-designed interfaces between each piece. Every boundary between layers is a place where information gets thrown away. You compress the world into bounding boxes or object poses or a symbolic plan, and whatever didn't fit that representation is gone. Errors also compound as you go down the stack. A small mistake in perception turns into a bad plan, which turns into a failed grasp.

What's happened with large vision-language models, and then vision-language-action models, is that we found one big pretrained network can absorb a lot of what used to be separate layers. The model already has a rich understanding of the world from internet-scale data: what objects are, how they relate, what "put the fruit in the bowl" means. So it makes sense to let that model see the pixels and the instruction directly and produce something much closer to actions, instead of forcing its understanding through a narrow symbolic bottleneck that an engineer designed.

So I see fewer layers as a consequence of a few things coming together. First, representations learned end to end are richer than hand-designed ones. Second, the bitter lesson: general methods that scale with data and compute keep beating carefully engineered pipelines. Third, fewer interfaces means less brittleness, so you don't have the classic failure where every module works in isolation but the system breaks at the seams.

That said, I don't think it collapses all the way to a single monolithic layer, at least not yet. There are real physical constraints. A large model reasoning about a scene can run at a few hertz, but dexterous control often needs much faster, reactive feedback. So in practice you still see something like a two-level split: a bigger model that does the semantic reasoning, task understanding, maybe planning, and a smaller, faster action component that turns that into smooth, high-frequency motor commands. It's like a "thinking" part and a "reflex" part. But even that split is learned and trained together rather than glued from hand-written modules.

The direction is clear, though. The stack keeps getting thinner, and the boundaries that remain exist because of latency, compute, and hardware, not because we think humans should design the intermediate representations. As models get faster and on-device compute improves, I'd expect even those remaining boundaries to blur further.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to understand it is that robotics has historically been this very layered stack, right? You'd have a perception module, then a state estimator, then a planner, then a motion planner, then a low-level controller. Each of those was its own research subfield with its own hand-designed interfaces. And the problem with that is every interface is a lossy bottleneck. The perception system has to decide what to output before it knows what the planner actually needs, and errors compound as you go down the stack.

What we've seen in language and vision is that when you have enough data and enough compute, the model learns better intermediate representations than the ones we design by hand. So the trend toward collapsing layers is really the robotics version of that same lesson. In Gemini Robotics the idea is you take a VLM that already understands the world semantically, and you fine-tune it so that it directly outputs actions, or you keep a very thin action decoder on top of it. The "thinking" and the "acting" are much closer together than they used to be.

Now I'd push back a little on the framing that it's purely fewer layers. There's still structure. In the Gemini Robotics work there's a split between the big backbone that does the reasoning and a smaller, faster component that runs on the robot and produces the actual motor commands at high frequency. That's not a conceptual layer in the old sense, it's more of a latency and compute constraint. You can't run a frontier model at fifty hertz on a robot arm, so you distill or you separate out the fast loop. So I'd say the layers that are disappearing are the semantic ones, the hand-coded abstractions, and the layers that remain are driven by physics and hardware.

The reason this works now and didn't work five years ago is really pretraining. The backbone comes in knowing what a mug is, knowing that liquids spill, knowing roughly what "put it on the shelf" means. You don't have to teach any of that through robot data, which is incredibly expensive to collect. The robot data just has to teach the grounding, how those concepts map onto this specific embodiment.

And the thing I find most exciting is that it changes what generalization looks like. In the old stack, if you wanted the robot to handle a new object, someone had to go fix the perception module. Now the model can often just do it because the knowledge was already there. The failure modes get more interesting too, they look more like language model failures, where the model understands the task but makes a weird physical mistake, rather than the classic robotics failure where the planner was never even given the right information.

So, short version, I see it as the field finally trusting end-to-end learning the way vision and language did, but with the honest caveat that real-time control still forces some architectural separation that isn't going away soon.

r002.rationale: It explains that hand-designed interfaces between robotics modules are lossy bottlenecks and says that thinking and acting are now much closer together in one model.

astra-6.text:
I think the broader trend is toward having fewer separately engineered stages between perception and action. Traditionally, you might have one system that interprets the scene, another that plans, and another that executes. Each interface introduces assumptions about what information the next stage needs, and those assumptions can become bottlenecks.

With a more integrated model, you can learn more of that mapping jointly: how what the robot sees, and what you ask it to do, should translate into movement. That’s appealing because understanding and action are closely coupled. What matters in an image depends on what you’re trying to do with it.

But I would distinguish that from saying the neural network itself necessarily has fewer layers. And I wouldn’t take it to mean that every part of a robot should become one model. You still have timing constraints, control requirements, and safety mechanisms. The interesting question is which boundaries help the system and which boundaries are artifacts of how we used to build it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the trend is toward fewer hand-designed boundaries between perception, reasoning, and action, rather than necessarily fewer neural network layers. Traditionally, a robotics system might have separate modules for detecting objects, estimating their poses, planning a motion, and executing it. Each interface creates assumptions about what information the next module needs, and you can lose useful information along the way.

With models like Gemini Robotics, the idea is to learn more of that mapping jointly: take in visual observations and language instructions and produce actions. That gives the model an opportunity to connect what it sees directly to what it needs to do, while sharing capabilities across tasks.

But I wouldn’t interpret that as saying every part of a robot should become one model. You still need to think carefully about control, latency, and safety. The interesting question is which abstractions help the system generalize and which ones are constraints we introduced because we couldn’t previously learn across them.
